persons.name: John Barney
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Barney, John' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). persons.name: O. Goss
persons.note: THE FORENAME IS A GUESS AT AN INITIAL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The advertisement gives 'Goss' with no initial. Andreas's table of first purchasers of canal lots carries an 'O. Goss, Washington Co. Vermont' buying on 3 September 1832, which is the only Goss in the volume near this date and place, and this record adopts that initial while grading the person derived because the identification is a reading and not a statement. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later.

persons.name: Silas B. Cobb
persons.note: IDENTIFIED, NOT PROVEN, AND ALREADY FLAGGED IN THE STRUCTURES LAYER. data/structures/goss_cobb_saddlery.json says in terms: 'Neither source connects the saddler to the carpenter in terms, so the identification is not made.' This household makes it, one grade down, because a minor arriving on 1 June 1833 and a Cobb advertising at Lake and Canal that November is a coherent single person and because leaving the initial unresolved loses a dated arrival. THE GRADE IS THE WARNING and a source that separates the two men should split this record. OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Cobb, Silas B. | 1833, May 29, | Montpelier, Vt. | 67 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Silas B. Cobb” (f1839_v0352, printed page 43, ward 2, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins S. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “S. B. Cobb”. 2 lot rows, $516.0 in all: block 10 lot 10 at $268.5 (f1839_lot0183, printed page 49); block 10 lot 11 at $247.5 (f1839_lot0184, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 of those rows prints the bidder as a ditto mark under the name above rather than the name itself; 2 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins S. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_lots_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Cobb, Stephen A, | Profession. | April 3, 1889.” (second_presb_0123, printed page 160), admitted 1889-04-03 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Cobb' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins S. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: SADDLERY IS THE TRADE THAT PROVES THE TOWN HAD TRAFFIC. Two saddle and harness makers advertising at Lake and Canal in 1833 - on the west side, on the road out of town - is evidence about wagons, teams and the overland trade that this dataset otherwise sees only through Ordinance 9's barrels in the street. THIS HOUSEHOLD MAKES AN IDENTIFICATION THE STRUCTURES LAYER DECLINED TO MAKE, one grade down and with the disagreement written on both persons; that asymmetry is deliberate and should be read as the residents layer proposing a reading, not as the dataset having changed its mind.

persons.name: R. Stewart
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'R. stewart' and 'RK, STEW ART' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the American of 13 June 1835, column 3; the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 32; the Democrat of 9 July 1834, column 7; the Democrat of 16 July 1834, column 7. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `attorney` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Royal Stewart,” (f1839_v0111, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Stewart' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins R. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 7 times, as “STEWART ROYAL”, 1836-06-20 to 6/22/1836: 7 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL35CHIOT, as printed); lot 1 of block 9 in the town the register codes CHIOTVO (L1BL9CHIOTVO, as printed); lot 2 of block 8 in the town the register codes CHIOTVO (L2BL8CHIOTVO, as printed); lot 2 of block 9 in the town the register codes CHIOTVO (L2BL9CHIOTVO, as printed); lot 3 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL2CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 38 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL38CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 37 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL37CHIOT, as printed), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $47560.00 (ls1470, ls1471, ls1472, ls1473, ls1474, ls1475, ls1476). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $47560.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: STEWART ROYAL matches R. Stewart: the forename names R. Stewart of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees as an initial only. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name R. Stewart as a attorney at Chicago 4 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

persons.name: Aaron Whitcomb
persons.note: KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Aaron Whitcomb' and 'n Whitcomb' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 28 January 1834, column 1, reprinted over 2 consecutive issues — dated 1834-01-28 to 1834-03-04. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).
